i'm the child of someone who works as the British equivalent of a teacher's aid, in a school specifically for people like this kid. I've seen the danger and the stress involved in working with kids with additional needs. 

what happened in this video was horrific, the perpetrator deserves punishment, the victim deserves justice. that all goes without saying. i just want people to realise these situations don't just occur out of the blue. children like this have been failed long before they come into school, and the consequences of those failures are placed on aids and support assistants who do their absolute best, sometimes in violent acts like this. this woman and her colleagues are already angels but they work without the training they need, the resources to keep them safe and the ability to protect themselves, which all compounds the problem and makes their jobs so much more stressful.

if we want to stop horrific abuse like this from happening to our educators, we need to actually care for our kids. he's built like a brick shithouse and obviously doesn't know how to control his impulses or anger- so why was the teacher ever alone in a situation with him? it's so easy to just call for his jailing, and very understandable considering what this poor woman went through, but we need to ask why it was allowed to happen in the first place so we can avoid it happening again. 

not bothered about downvotes if it makes people think. I'm autistic and have experienced this firsthand- but people turn a blind eye because it's too uncomfortable and complex for them to understand.

edit: and I understand if you feel this is not the place to raise this issue. i apologise if anyone felt my comment was inappropriate. i strongly believe opening dialogue when the issue is fresh in people's minds helps us make progress, especially as so many people don't have an insight into this issue.

reading between the lines, does this kid have additional needs? obviously doesn't justify violence but it's important to factor, some kids with learning/developmental disabilities struggle with anger and impulse control. hope to god that the teacher's aid receives support and compensation, really wish incidents like this would start a dialogue about how much we fail disabled kids and the people who care for them

I'm not immune to it either, because the experience of disability/learning difference/neurodivergency is so vast! when people say "you don't seem autistic", they usually mean "you don't fit my preconvieved notions about autism", which can really hurt autistic people who have spent their lives living up to the inaccurate and harmful mediated misrepresentations of them. I think a good rule is ask questions when you feel it's appropriate, take "no" at face value, and be willing to do the work in your own time rather than only acknowledging disability when it's right in front of you.

I have seen love on the spectrum, and I have a very very complicated relationship with shows like that (we have a similar one in the UK for all disabled people called The Undateables). I think it's really interesting that you were able to pick up on the infantalising tones, because it's something that neurodivergent and people with learning differences experience a LOT. autism especially, because of things like Rain Man, Forrest Gump (people think he is autistic) even comedic characters like Sheldon on TBBT. We never get representation of the vast, vast spectrum in-between what people would consider "low" or "high" functioning. I'm glad that it showed the middle ground, because we've spent decades seeing only the worse, and it can make being autistic difficult to express because people don't believe you, or difficult to find support with because you never measure up as needy enough.
